What does this data measure?Germany's wholesale price index measures changes in prices charged by wholesalers to retailers and other businesses. It offers an early indication of cost pressures in the supply chain, which can eventually feed through to consumer inflation.

Why does it matter to markets?Germany is the the euro area's largest economy, making wholesale prices a useful gauge of underlying inflation risks. A sustained increase in wholesale costs could complicate the ECB's efforts to contain inflation, particularly if businesses pass higher costs on to consumers.

How does it fit into the current economic landscape?Wholesale inflation has been accelerating, with September's annual increase reaching its strongest pace since early 2023. item.title: Japan prime minister Takaichi fires another verbal warning as USD/JPY flirts with the 160 level
item.description:
Knock, knock. Who's there? Japan's intervention warning, of course. With USD/JPY flirting with the 160.00 level again this week, Tokyo is making sure that traders know that someone is watching.

Japan's prime minister Takaich is the latest to chime in with some comments, saying that:

  • Does not want to comment on exchange rate levels
  • In close contact with US financial authorities on the exchange rate
  • Will work to maintain an orderly FX market
  • Exchange rates are determined by various factors
  • Economic and fiscal policies are not aimed at manipulating exchange rates
  • Will manage economic and fiscal policies while closely monitoring market developments

It's all fairly familiar language but as always, it is more about the timing of the commentary.

USD/JPY briefly poked above the 160.00 mark in trading yesterday and is hovering just below the figure level again today. So, that puts traders back in dangerously familiar territory - especially after Japan's intervention play over the summer.

If you need a reminder, Tokyo had already shown proof that Washington is willing to lend a helping hand. So, that makes Takaichi's reference to close US coordination more than just diplomatic pleasantries.

In any case, just be wary that crossing the 160.00 level isn't some magical line that automatically triggers intervention. As mentioned before, Japanese authorities care more so about the speed and disorderliness of currency moves, not merely the exchange rate itself.

That being said, USD/JPY sellers definitely have their work cut out for them. The dollar's resurgence this week is something noteworthy, being driven by rising US yields and more hawkish Fed expectations. As such, verbal warnings alone won't be something that can easily undo that interest rate advantage.

As such, that brings us back to a familiar game of who blinks first. Dollar bulls certainly have the momentum on the week but Tokyo has already shown its willingness to act this year. But as USD/JPY continues to test the limits near or just above the 160.00 mark, something's gotta give eventually.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: US bond market cracks resurface as higher for longer fears return to haunt Wall Street
item.description:
Oh, would you look at who's back to spoil the party this week? Well, it is the bond market of course. And surprise, surprise, it's bringing along the same old problems that Wall Street has been trying to sweep under the rug over the past week.

For all the optimism about easing geopolitical tensions earlier this week, we're right back to square one or perhaps even taking one step back now. 10-year Treasury yields have climbed up to 5.12% while 30-year yields are pushing 5.45% as we look to end the week.

It's rather amusing that we're still running in circles, confronting the same issues that drove yields to multi-decade highs in the first place. I mean, was anything ever really fixed?

Oil prices may have fallen at the start of the week, but fresh reports of strikes in Iran and Trump declaring that the US doesn't need a deal with Tehran have quickly poured cold water on hopes of any lasting reprieve. Yup, pretty much a case of déjà vu and that is nothing new when it comes to the US-Iran conflict. We've been down this road one too many a time over the last eight months.

As such, that leaves the threat of another energy-driven inflation shock hanging over markets. And it's not as though the latest inflation numbers are giving the Fed much room to breathe either.

The October CPI report saw headline prices rise 0.4% against expectations of 0.3%, while core inflation also surprised higher at 0.3%. Well, so much for the thought of inflation quietly disappearing into the background.

When you put those two together, the higher for longer narrative is proving to be rather stubborn. And the backdrop gets even more uncomfortable when you have Washington continuing to pile on debt at a time when borrowing costs are already painfully high.

The latest numbers this week showed that the US posted a record $404 billion budget deficit for October, up from $284 billion a year earlier. That's hardly reassuring when the government needs investors to keep financing its spending. And it's evident that those very same investors aren't exactly waiting in line to lend money to the government. The latest $25 billion 30-year Treasury auction saw the bid-to-cover ratio slip to 2.36 from 2.54 previously, underscoring weaker demand at the long-end of the curve.

The trouble with all this is that it goes beyond just what the Fed does next.

At this stage, investors want greater compensation for the uncertainty of holding government debt. That is especially the case as inflation risks continue to linger and Washington's borrowing needs are showing little signs of slowing down.

In essence, that's the term premium that the bond market is talking about. Or to put it more simply, if I'm lending you money for 30 years, you'd better make it worth my while.

Now, a Fed pause might provide some temporary relief for broader markets. However, that won't magically make those bigger picture concerns disappear in an instant.

So, what does this mean for Wall Street?

Well, tech shares have been under the microscope in recent weeks and the latest developments here will only increase the scrutiny on them moving forward.

In the past few weeks, investors were already getting nervous about the enormous AI infrastructure spending and whether those investments could eventually justify their lofty expectations. And Nvidia's recent woes have only shaken confidence further.

So now, you're adding in another problem to that. Or should I say, a familiar problem that we have been talking about since August and September i.e. surging bond yields. Higher Treasury yields will make future earnings less valuable in today's money, while also raising financing costs for companies spending heavily on growth. That's a troubling thought that is coming at the wrong time when investors are already questioning how much they're willing to pay for the AI dream.

All that being said, I'm not suggesting that a major crash in tech stocks is inevitable. But with 10-year yields starting to nudge back up above 5% again, it is worth keeping in mind that tech stocks don't quite have as much breathing room as they once did in terms of trying to withstand another push higher in borrowing costs.

As much as markets want to celebrate falling oil prices or the prospect of an eventual Fed pivot, I struggle to see how either solves the fundamental problems weighing on bonds. We're still dealing with sticky inflation, persistent fiscal deficits and the fact that investors are demanding more to finance US debt.

And until something changes, I reckon the bond market will keep finding ways to haunt Wall Street about the same old problems that never really went away.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

Rising bets on further Federal Reserve rate hikes spread through Asian markets on Friday. Japanese government bonds slumped, the yen stayed close to 160 per dollar and bitcoin fell below $69,000. Regional stocks gave back much of an early rebound, as concern over Nvidia’s leadership change continued to weigh on AI-linked shares.

Fed and rates

Japan’s 10-year yield rose about 7 basis points to around 2.87%, at the day’s high. JGBs followed US Treasuries, which posted a second straight session of losses as traders added to bets on more forceful Fed tightening. The US 10-year yield traded near 5.13%. New York Fed President John Williams said overnight that inflation remains stubbornly high and that the Fed will need to act over time to bring it back to 2%. He described the US economy as getting stronger but not overheating. His remarks followed this week’s hotter-than-expected October consumer price data, after which markets priced a high probability of a quarter-point hike at the Fed’s 9 December decision, along with an outside chance of a half-point move.

Yen and Japan

Dollar-yen traded near 159.90. Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said she is seeing one-sided, rapid currency moves and will communicate with the US Treasury to respond appropriately, adding that the two countries set out a shared stance on currencies at their summit. She declined to comment on intervention. Her remarks came after the New York Fed confirmed that the US Treasury bought yen in July, its first yen-buying intervention since 1998, alongside Japan’s own intervention. Katayama also said the government will bring forward winter subsidies for utility bills to ease energy costs for households.

Oil and geopolitics

Brent traded near $95.70 and WTI near $88.40, both slightly lower. That was despite a claim by Iran’s Revolutionary Guards that they destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain in response to an attack on a telecommunications tower in Sirik. The claim could not be independently verified, and there was no immediate US comment. The Guards also warned companies working with the US over oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. Barclays said the market is too relaxed about the risks, with Middle East flows still around 85% of pre-war levels and inventories outside China depressed. Goldman Sachs also said risks to its oil forecast are skewed to the upside. Airlines are feeling the pressure as fuel hedges struck before the war expire, with jet fuel near $148 a barrel.

Asian equities

The Nikkei 225 was up about 0.8% near 61,300 in afternoon trade, down from a gain of about 1.4% at midday. The Topix rose about 0.3%. The Kospi reversed an early 2% advance to trade about 0.7% lower near 5,300, with SK Hynix down more than 2% and Samsung Electronics off about 0.6%. The Kosdaq held a gain of about 1.5%. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell about 1% to near 23,770, while the Shanghai Composite edged up about 0.2%.

Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia chief executive remained the main drag on AI names. Nvidia shares fell about 3% in extended US trading, and South Korea’s Naver also slipped. Citi said investors may look to AMD, Arista and Broadcom as alternatives. In China, SMIC reported record third-quarter revenue of about $3.19 billion and more than doubled its profit. Its co-chief executive said full-year revenue should top $12 billion, but warned that tight supplies of chipmaking equipment could disrupt capital spending.

AI and tech

Earnings continued to support the AI spending story. Cisco beat forecasts and raised its full-year outlook on AI networking demand from hyperscalers. Applied Materials guided above consensus, and Cerebras reported record revenue and a backlog of around $26 billion. Goldman Sachs forecast that annualised AI-related spending will reach $1.4 trillion by the end of 2027, nearly 4% of the US economy. ByteDance plans a share buyback valuing it at about $400 billion, according to a report.

Gold and crypto

Gold rose about 0.7% to near $3,914 and silver traded around $50. BlackRock described the outlook for gold as more balanced, with central bank buying offsetting pressure from higher real yields and a firm dollar. Société Générale expects January’s commodity index rebalancing to add about $3.3 billion of net buying in gold futures. Bitcoin dropped more than 6% to below $69,000, as US spot bitcoin ETFs extended a run of outflows that has taken November’s withdrawals to close to $2 billion.

Australia and New Zealand

The Australian dollar traded near 0.6800 and the New Zealand dollar near 0.5540. The yield advantage that Australian 10-year bonds held over Treasuries earlier in the year has disappeared, with the Fed leaning toward hikes and the RBA appearing to be on hold. UBS expects the RBA to keep policy restrictive, with no rate cuts before late 2027. In New Zealand, the manufacturing PMI eased to 54.9 in October but marked a 16th straight month of expansion.

Coming up

Anthropic is due to price its IPO on 18 November, with Nasdaq trading set to begin the following day. The deal is reported to be about six times oversubscribed.

item.title: Bitcoin dipped under $70K, first time since August
item.description:
Bitcoin’s slide back toward $70,000 has no single headline trigger. The pressure is coming from several directions at once, and most of it is about money leaving rather than news arriving. Support appears just above $66K.

The clearest signal is in exchange-traded funds. US spot bitcoin ETFs have recorded five straight sessions of outflows, taking November’s withdrawals to close to $2 billion and pushing net flows for 2026 into negative territory. Almost all of that has come from BlackRock’s iShares fund. That suggests larger institutional holders are reducing exposure, rather than retail traders panicking.

Rates are doing the rest. This week’s hot US inflation report has markets pricing a high chance of a Federal Reserve hike in December. Fed officials, including New York Fed President John Williams, have said there is more work to do.

  • Fed’s Williams says inflation stubbornly high and Fed still has work to do on policy

Higher real yields and a dollar near multi-month highs raise the cost of holding assets that pay no income, the same force that has pushed gold sharply lower this year. Bitcoin is also caught in the unwinding of the broader “debasement trade”: investors who bought hard assets because of worries about government debt are now focused on tighter policy instead.

There is also a liquidity squeeze from equities. Crypto and AI-linked stocks draw on the same pool of speculative capital, and the recent selloff in technology stocks has spilled into digital assets. Next week’s Anthropic IPO, which with its private placement could absorb close to $90 billion, may also be drawing money away from other risk assets.

Finally, leverage is making the moves bigger. Forced liquidations of leveraged positions topped $700 million in a single session this week, turning orderly selling into sharper drops. With $72,000 already lost, traders are watching whether $70,000 holds. If it doesn’t, the mid-$60,000s are seen as the next area of support.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Iran’s Guards claim strike on US radar in Bahrain, warn firms over Hormuz oil trade
item.description:
The claim is unverified, but it adds to the geopolitical risk premium in crude after a week in which Brent and WTI fell about 7%. The warning to companies matters most for oil: any hint that tanker operators, charterers or insurers will step back from Hormuz could tighten flows that are still below pre-war levels and push freight and war-risk insurance costs higher. Light speculative positioning means a confirmed escalation could trigger a sharp short-covering bounce. A US denial, or no follow-up, would likely see the move fade, as with past episodes. Higher oil would also feed inflation worries and support Fed hike expectations.

---

Earlier:

  • Barclays sees oil risks skewed higher with Middle East flows still 15% below pre-war

Iran’s Guards claim another hit on US assets in Bahrain. The claim is unverified, but the warning to companies over Hormuz oil shipments is the part oil traders should watch.

Summary:

  • The IRGC says it targeted and destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain
  • It says the strike responded to an air attack on a telecommunications tower in Sirik, on Iran’s Hormuz coast
  • The claim could not be independently verified, and there was no immediate US or Bahraini comment
  • The IRGC warned of unlimited confrontation if attacks are repeated
  • It also warned that companies working with the US over Hormuz oil shipments face tougher penalties
  • Sirik’s radar and telecoms sites have been hit before, with earlier tit-for-tat strikes on US facilities in Bahrain

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it had targeted and destroyed a US military early-warning radar in Bahrain, in what it called retaliation for an air attack on a telecommunications tower in the southern Iranian town of Sirik. Iranian state media carried the claim on Friday, and it could not be independently verified. There was no immediate comment from the US military or Bahrain.

In its statement, the IRGC said its aerospace force carried out the strike a few hours earlier. It called the strike a serious warning to the United States to halt what it described as aerial provocations and oil smuggling in the Strait of Hormuz. It said its forces were fully prepared for unlimited confrontation if such actions were repeated, and warned that companies cooperating with the US would face more severe penalties.

The claim fits a familiar pattern. Sirik, on Iran’s coast near the Strait of Hormuz, hosts part of the radar and communications network that monitors the shipping lane. Its telecoms infrastructure has been struck before during the conflict, and the IRGC has answered earlier strikes by targeting US facilities in Bahrain and elsewhere in the Gulf. In past episodes, US Central Command has disputed some Iranian claims of damage to its assets.

For oil markets, the more significant part of the statement may be the warning to companies. The reference to oil smuggling and penalties for firms working with the US points to continued pressure on tanker traffic through Hormuz, where Middle East export flows are still below pre-war levels. Any sign that shipping companies or insurers are pulling back would quickly feed into prices. Brent and WTI have fallen roughly 7% this week as some traders bet on the stalemate continuing calmly.

The next things to watch are whether US Central Command or Bahrain confirms or rejects the Iranian account, whether the US responds further around Hormuz, and whether tanker movements and freight rates react. Until then, the claim adds to the risk premium rather than directly changing the supply picture.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

  • Requests are not guaranteed, buyers must be ready to take every share they request, and fast flipping can limit future access
  • US IPOs have risen almost 20% on average on day one since 1975, a gain that mostly goes to those allocated shares at the offer price

Anthropic is setting aside an unusually large share of its IPO for individual investors. But orders are running at about six times the shares available, so most retail buyers who put in a request are likely to receive only a fraction of what they ask for, and some will get nothing.

The company has said it expects up to 20% of the 825 million shares on offer to go to retail investors. That is roughly double the 5% to 10% that individuals typically receive in a large US listing. Some of those shares will come through the main underwriting group, led by Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley. The rest will come through online brokers named in the filing: Charles Schwab, Fidelity, Robinhood and its TradePMR unit, SoFi, and Morgan Stanley’s E*Trade. Pricing is expected on 18 November, with Nasdaq trading under the ticker ANT due to begin the next day.

Demand is the main obstacle. Bloomberg News reported on Thursday that the offering has drawn about six times as many orders as there are shares, and that bankers have told prospective investors existing backers will be prioritised. The same reporting has fuelled talk that the price could be set above the $70 to $78 range.

Getting in the queue is also not simple. Each broker sets its own rules. Fidelity requires at least $25,000 in assets with the firm, while Schwab has cut its threshold to $50,000. Brokers typically divide shares on a pro rata basis, in fixed amounts or by lottery. Anthropic’s own IPO page makes clear that a request does not guarantee a purchase. Investors should be prepared to buy every share they ask for, and allocations are confirmed on the first day of trading. Some brokers also penalise customers who sell IPO shares quickly. Fidelity reportedly warns that selling within 15 days can limit access to future deals.

For those who miss out, the first trade may not be the best one. Academic data show US IPOs have risen by nearly 20% on average on their first day since 1975. That gain mostly goes to those who receive shares at the offer price. One research firm estimates individual investors could buy a record $250 million of Anthropic stock on the first day of trading, more than double the retail buying seen in SpaceX’s debut in June. Buying at the open means paying any first-day premium on top of a valuation that is already high relative to sales. Historically, the most richly valued IPOs have tended to lag over the following years.

The broader lesson is that a bigger retail allocation improves access, but it does not guarantee a good entry price. Robinhood set aside a large slice of its own 2021 listing for its customers, and the shares fell below the offer price on the first day. Popular IPOs can disappoint early buyers too.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Airlines face higher fuel bills as pre-war hedges expire and jet fuel holds near $150
item.description:
Expiring hedges mean airline earnings will become more exposed to swings in crude, keeping pressure on airline stocks even after this week’s pullback in oil. Any renewed jump in Brent on Middle East shipping risk would now hit airline margins harder, especially in Asia, where fuel’s share of costs has risen to about a third. If airlines lock in new cover at current prices, the hedging demand could also support the deferred part of the oil curve. Higher fares and new fuel surcharges add to inflation pressures that are already keeping central banks hawkish, supporting the case for higher-for-longer rates.

---

  • Earlier:Fed’s Williams says inflation stubbornly high and Fed still has work to do on policy

---

The fuel hedges that protected airlines through the first months of the Iran war are expiring, so carriers must lock in costly new cover or take on more risk. Either way, passengers will probably pay more.

Summary:

  • Fuel hedges set at pre-war prices are expiring, leaving airlines more exposed to high jet fuel costs
  • Jet fuel is near $148 a barrel, down from nearly $180 at the end of October but well above about $85 before the war
  • Fuel is now about a third of Asia-Pacific airline operating costs, up from a quarter last year
  • Executives disagree: Air Astana sees a new normal, while JAL and ANA expect prices to fluctuate or stabilise
  • Singapore Airlines’ fuel bill jumped 56%, cutting operating profit by 29% despite record revenue
  • Higher fares and new surcharges risk denting demand and adding to inflation

Airlines are losing the protection that shielded them through the first months of the Iran war. Fuel hedges struck at pre-war prices are expiring, and carriers face a costly choice over whether to lock in new cover at far higher levels. The squeeze is sharpest in Asia-Pacific, but airlines worldwide face the same dilemma. It is feeding through to higher fares at a time when inflation is already a problem for central banks.

Jet fuel in Singapore, the region’s benchmark, is trading at around $148 a barrel, Reuters reported. That is down from nearly $180 at the end of October but still far above the roughly $85 seen before the conflict began in late February. According to the Association of Asia Pacific Airlines, fuel now accounts for about a third of airline operating costs in the region. Global industry body IATA put fuel at about a quarter of costs last year.

The group’s director general, Wong Hong, described hedging as a very tricky dilemma. He said airlines with cover in place over the past six to eight months had done well, but now face renewing it at much higher prices. Deciding whether to hedge again is effectively a bet on where oil goes next, and executives gathered in Kuala Lumpur this week were divided.

Air Astana’s chief executive, Ibrahim Canliel, said the industry faces a new normal, with Brent likely to stay around $90 to $100. Japan Airlines expects prices to swing up and down and is budgeting for a worst case of $160 a barrel for jet fuel. All Nippon Airways expects fuel costs this financial year to run about 100 billion yen (around $625 million) above plan, though it expects the market to stabilise in the second half.

Singapore Airlines shows the limits of hedging. Its fuel bill jumped 56% to nearly S$4 billion in the six months to September, cutting operating profit by 29% despite record revenue. Before hedging, it paid about $170 a barrel. Hedging gains of around S$730 million brought that down to roughly $145.

Passengers are now carrying more of the cost. JAL will introduce a domestic fuel surcharge for the first time from April. Wong warned that fares cannot keep rising indefinitely, noting that regional passenger growth was negative from April to August and that capacity cuts are a clear risk.

The wider concern is inflation. Airfares feed directly into consumer price indices, and fuel surcharges spread the oil shock well beyond household energy bills. US consumer prices are already running hotter than expected, and central banks from the Fed to the Bank of Japan are focused on persistent price pressures. The airline industry’s struggle with fuel is another way high oil prices are keeping inflation sticky. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: SMIC co-CEO sees 2026 revenue topping $12 billion as AI demand stretches chip upcycle
item.description:
The results and full-year outlook support the argument that AI demand is spilling over from leading-edge chips into mature-node foundries. That is constructive for China’s chip supply chain, and it may help steady sentiment toward SMIC’s Hong Kong shares after a steep sell-off. The warning about equipment delivery times points to strong demand for tools, a positive read-through for chip equipment makers that fits Applied Materials’ upbeat outlook this week. The Q4 margin guidance below Q3’s 29.9% will temper enthusiasm. So will continued questions over how quickly AI spending pays off, which could cap any rebound across Asian chip stocks.

---

SMIC’s co-CEO expects AI to keep the chip boom going for longer and full-year revenue to top $12bn. His warning that equipment shortages could disrupt spending shows how tight the supply chain has become.

Summary:

  • Co-CEO Zhao Haijun expects full-year revenue above $12bn, up nearly 30%, with gross margin around 26%, about 5 points higher than last year
  • He says AI demand could extend the semiconductor upcycle, alongside the ongoing localisation of China’s chip supply chain
  • Tight global equipment supply and longer delivery times may disrupt full-year capex, though not this year’s capacity expansion
  • Q3 revenue rose 34% to a record $3.19bn, and net profit more than doubled to about $428m, beating forecasts near $397m
  • Q3 gross margin of 29.9% topped guidance; Q4 guidance is revenue up 4% to 6% sequentially with margin of 26% to 28%
  • SMIC’s Hong Kong shares fell 32% in Q3 and about another 20% so far this quarter

SMIC co-chief executive Zhao Haijun said the company expects full-year revenue to top $12 billion, up nearly 30% from last year. He argued that demand from artificial intelligence could extend the current semiconductor upcycle. Speaking on the company’s third-quarter earnings call, he also warned that tight global supplies of chipmaking equipment could disrupt the timing of its capital spending.

Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp, better known as SMIC, is China’s largest contract chipmaker. It was founded in 2000 and is based in Shanghai. Like Taiwan’s TSMC, it is a foundry: it makes chips that other companies design, rather than selling chips under its own name. Most of its output is mature-node chips, the older but widely used technology found in power management, connectivity, cars and consumer electronics. SMIC is listed in Hong Kong and on Shanghai’s STAR Market, and is central to Beijing’s push for chip self-sufficiency. The United States placed it on its Entity List in 2020, restricting its access to American technology, including the most advanced chipmaking tools. That makes it a closely watched gauge of how far China can advance its chip industry under those controls.

Zhao said gross margin for the year should come in around 26%, about 5 percentage points higher than last year, even as total depreciation rises by roughly 30%. He described two near-term certainties for the industry. The first is AI demand extending the cycle and changing how growth plays out. The second is the large-scale, ongoing localisation of China’s chip supply chain. SMIC plans to rely on its ties with Chinese customers, expand capacity in line with their demand and prioritise higher-value products to protect cash flow through the cycle.

The equipment warning is the main caveat. Zhao said supply chains for chipmaking tools are generally tight, with longer delivery times and uncertainty over when some machines will arrive. He said that will not derail this year’s capacity expansion, but it may disrupt how capital spending is carried out over the full year.

His comments followed another record quarter. Revenue rose 34% from a year earlier to about $3.19 billion, after topping $3 billion for the first time in the second quarter. Net profit more than doubled to around $428 million, ahead of analysts’ forecasts of about $397 million. Gross margin reached 29.9%, beating the company’s own guidance of 26% to 28% on higher wafer prices and a more profitable product mix. The fabs ran at about 97% utilisation.

SMIC is benefiting from AI indirectly. The leading foundries are devoting more capacity to advanced AI chips, so customers in China and abroad are turning to China for mature-node chips. These are used for power management, connectivity and other supporting roles in data centres and consumer electronics. TrendForce data show SMIC’s global foundry market share rose to 5.4% in the second quarter, closing in on Samsung’s 5.9%, though both remain far behind TSMC.

For the fourth quarter, SMIC guided for revenue growth of 4% to 6% from the third quarter, with gross margin of 26% to 28%. The results now face a sceptical market. The company’s Hong Kong shares fell 32% in the third quarter and have lost about another 20% this quarter, as investors question how quickly heavy AI spending will pay off. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold set for $3.3bn of index fund buying in January as rebalancing flips in its favour
item.description:
The rebalancing gives gold a known (ps. be careful of known knowns in markets ...) source of demand in the second week of January. That could make traders reluctant to press short positions into year-end and encourage some to buy ahead of the window. Because the buying is concentrated in April futures, the spread between February and April contracts could see unusual moves while funds roll. Silver’s smaller and less liquid market could feel its estimated $2.5bn more sharply. The reverse applies to energy, where index funds will be trimming exposure after this year’s oil-led gains, a modest headwind for crude while the Middle East supply risks persist.

---

After a year of selling pressure, gold gets mechanical support in January as index funds rebalance toward it, though $3bn of buying is a short-term prop rather than a lasting turnaround.

Summary:

  • Société Générale expects the annual commodity index rebalancing to bring about $3.3bn of net buying in gold futures and around $2.5bn in silver
  • The reweighting runs from 8 to 14 January, with gold’s share of the Bloomberg Commodity Index rising about 3 percentage points and its S&P GSCI weighting about 1 point
  • Funds are expected to sell around $17bn of February gold futures and buy about $20.5bn of April contracts
  • April buying could exceed half of normal daily volume in that contract during the window
  • Assets tracking the two main commodity benchmarks are around $160bn, down from a peak above $200bn
  • Société Générale keeps 10% allocations to both gold and broader commodities in its multi-asset strategy

Index funds that had to sell gold at the start of this year are set to become buyers in January, giving the metal a technical boost after a bruising run. Société Générale estimates that the annual reweighting of the big commodity benchmarks will produce net purchases of about $3.3 billion of gold futures, and roughly another $2.5 billion of silver.

The flows mirror this year’s commodity scorecard. Energy has been the standout as the Middle East conflict disrupted supply, while precious metals have slumped. Gold now trades around $3,870 an ounce, after setting a record near $5,400 in January. Funds that track the Bloomberg Commodity Index and the S&P GSCI must return to fixed target weights each year, so they trim the winners and top up the laggards. By the bank’s estimate, that means lifting gold’s share of the Bloomberg index by around 3 percentage points and its GSCI weighting by about 1 point. The process runs from 8 to 14 January.

Much of the activity will come through a roll from one contract month to another. Société Générale expects index funds to sell around $17 billion of February gold futures and buy roughly $20.5 billion of April contracts, which leaves the net $3.3 billion. The April buying alone could make up more than half of normal daily volume in that contract during the window. That is enough to be felt in a market that has struggled for momentum.

The backdrop for passive commodity investing has also strengthened. Assets tracking the two main benchmarks rose from roughly $147 billion at the start of 2026 to more than $200 billion at the peak, before easing to around $160 billion this month. The Bloomberg index accounts for the larger share. Precious metals are also taking a bigger share of these portfolios over time: their target weighting in the GSCI is rising to 10% for 2027, from about 4% in 2023.

Société Générale’s view is not only about flows. Its multi-asset strategy, updated in September, kept a 10% allocation to gold and another 10% to broader commodities.

Still, a few billion dollars of mechanical buying is a short-term support rather than a turning point. With markets pricing further Fed tightening, and higher real yields weighing on assets that pay no income, gold will need more than January’s index reshuffle to recover.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ByteDance plans $6bn share buyback at about $400 billion valuation, up 20% in a year
item.description:
The buyback gives a fresh benchmark for valuing Chinese tech and large private AI-linked companies. That could support sentiment toward listed Chinese internet peers and toward investors with ByteDance exposure, such as SoftBank. A 20% rise in the company’s own valuation suggests management is confident in its advertising and AI businesses despite the geopolitical risk around TikTok. Setting the price below some secondary-market marks also suggests a conservative approach, which may limit how far the news lifts valuations of comparable companies.

-

Earlier:

  • Anthropic IPO targets around $1 trillion valuation, half the $2 trillion once whispered

-

ByteDance is raising its own valuation by a fifth to about $400 billion but still pricing below what some outside investors have paid, a confident but cautious mark for one of the world’s biggest private companies.

Summary:

  • ByteDance plans to buy back up to $6bn of shares from existing investors
  • The buyback values the company at about $400bn, around 20% above the valuation used a year ago
  • Valuations in past buybacks have risen steadily, from about $268bn in late 2023 to around $330bn last year
  • A minority-stake deal late last year reportedly valued ByteDance at about $480bn
  • The buyback gives investors a way to cash out of a company that has never listed

ByteDance, the Chinese owner of TikTok, plans to buy back up to $6 billion of shares from existing investors at a valuation of about $400 billion, The Information reported, citing a letter to shareholders and a person familiar with the matter. That is about 20% above the valuation used in the company’s previous buyback a year ago.

The rise fits the company’s recent pattern. ByteDance runs regular buybacks, which are a rare official price for one of the world’s most valuable private companies. Earlier reports show that price climbing steadily: from about $268 billion in late 2023, to around $300 billion a year later, to roughly $330 billion in last year’s round.

Even so, the new figure is below some outside valuations. A minority-stake deal late last year reportedly valued ByteDance at about $480 billion. That suggests the buyback price is set cautiously compared with what some investors have been willing to pay.

For shareholders, the buyback is a way to cash in their stake in a company that has never listed. The valuation reflects the strength of its core advertising business and growing interest in its AI work, including its Doubao chatbot.

The deal also comes in a busy week for AI valuations, with Anthropic set to price its IPO next week at around $1 trillion. Taken together, the two show how far private tech valuations have run. They also show how differently investors value an established profit-making platform and a fast-growing AI developer. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Japan’s Katayama warns of one-sided yen moves near 160, will coordinate with US Treasury
item.description:
Katayama’s comments make intervention a more serious risk for anyone pushing dollar-yen above 160, especially as the US has now been confirmed as a willing partner. Expect choppy, headline-driven trading around that level, with dealers alert to any reports of rate checks. The underlying pressure on the yen remains, though, as rising Fed hike expectations keep rate differentials in the dollar’s favour. Oil matters too: higher crude prices raise Japan’s import bill and add to selling pressure on the yen, which is partly why Tokyo is bringing forward energy subsidies.

---

Earlier:

  • US Treasury bought yen in July, its first intervention since 1998, as yen nears 160 again

---

With the yen back near 160, Katayama is reminding markets that Tokyo and Washington are working together on currencies, and that both have intervened before.

Summary:

  • Finance Minister Katayama says she is seeing one-sided, rapid moves in currency markets
  • She will communicate with the US Treasury and respond appropriately
  • She says the US and Japan shared a common stance on foreign exchange at their summit
  • She declined to comment on intervention records
  • The government is bringing forward winter utility subsidies, funded from reserve funds
  • The yen is back near 160 per dollar, the level that triggered joint US-Japan intervention in the summer

Main article: Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama stepped up her warnings over the yen’s slide, saying she is seeing one-sided and rapid moves in currency markets and will stay in contact with the US Treasury to respond appropriately. Her comments come as the yen trades back near 160 per dollar, the level that drew joint US-Japan intervention in the summer.

Katayama said the US and Japan set out a shared stance on foreign exchange at their summit, signalling that Tokyo sees Washington as aligned on the need to curb disorderly moves. She declined to comment on intervention records. That came shortly after the New York Fed disclosed that the US Treasury bought yen in July, its first yen-buying intervention since 1998, acting alongside Japan’s Ministry of Finance.

The wording matters. Japanese officials typically use terms like “one-sided” and “rapid” when their concern is growing. Naming coordination with the US Treasury adds weight, because Washington has now shown it is willing to put its own money behind the yen. Japan’s vice finance minister for international affairs, Atsushi Mimura, gave a similar message on Thursday, warning that it was too early to forget the summer’s intervention.

The yen’s renewed weakness reflects a familiar gap. A resilient US economy, stubborn inflation and rising expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike in December are supporting the dollar. The Bank of Japan, which raised rates in June and September, is widely expected to hike again in December. Until that gap narrows, officials are relying on words, and the threat of action, to slow the yen’s fall.

Katayama also said the government has decided to bring forward subsidies for household utility bills this winter, paid for from reserve funds. The move aims to protect households from high energy costs. Elevated oil prices have pushed those costs up, and the weak yen makes them worse, because Japan imports almost all of its energy.

For markets, the comments make it riskier for traders to push dollar-yen through 160. With both Tokyo and Washington signalling they are ready to act, the risk of another round of intervention is likely to keep the pair volatile around that level in the weeks before the BOJ’s December meeting. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Barclays sees oil risks skewed higher with Middle East flows still 15% below pre-war
item.description:
Barclays’ view goes against the recent selling in crude. It suggests the roughly 7% fall in Brent and WTI over the past week has gone further than the data support while flows and inventories stay tight. Light speculative positioning means a renewed Hormuz incident or a stalled diplomatic track could set off a sharp short-covering rally. The long Brent calendar spread recommendation reflects a bet that tight prompt supply will keep the curve in backwardation, with near-dated prices above later ones. Higher oil would also keep inflation and central bank hike expectations elevated, adding to pressure on rate-sensitive assets.

---

Barclays argues that oil doesn’t need a new shock to rise: with Hormuz flows still short, stocks depressed and traders under-positioned, simply continuing the stalemate is enough to tilt the risks higher.

Summary:

  • Barclays sees near-term oil price risks skewed to the upside, with a US-Iran diplomatic breakthrough still out of reach
  • Front-month Brent and WTI have each fallen about 7% since the bank’s previous update a week earlier
  • Direct Hormuz exports averaged about 9 mb/d in the week to 31 October, or nearly 18 mb/d including bypass routes, about 23% below pre-war
  • On a 30-day average, Middle East flows are around 85% of pre-war levels
  • Inventories outside China remain well below normal, and most strategic reserve releases are over
  • Demand from China and India is recovering and speculative positioning is light; Barclays keeps its forecasts and its long Brent calendar spread call

Barclays says oil markets are too relaxed about the risks ahead and sees prices skewed higher in the near term, even after a fresh slide in crude. In its latest Energy Sigma note, titled “Status quo”, the bank argues that a diplomatic breakthrough in US-Iran tensions remains out of reach, while traders are not positioned for the current stalemate to continue.

The call comes despite weak prices. Barclays noted that front-month Brent and WTI futures have each fallen about 7% since its previous update a week earlier, but said the data released since then all point the same way. In its view, diplomacy is continuing but an imminent deal looks unlikely.

The first pressure point is the Strait of Hormuz. A recent rise in attacks on shipping has slowed the recovery in Middle East flows. The bank said direct net exports through the Strait averaged about 9 million barrels per day in the week to 31 October. Ship-to-ship transfers and pipelines that bypass the Strait lifted the total to nearly 18 million barrels per day, still about 23% below pre-war levels. Flows briefly exceeded pre-war volumes in mid-October despite the blockade of Iran, but that did not last. On a 30-day average, Middle East flows were close to 19.5 million barrels per day at the end of October, around 85% of pre-war levels.

Barclays’ bigger concern is stockpiles. Inventories have stabilised but are not rebuilding. Global inventories outside China remain well below their usual range, and most strategic reserve releases are now over. The bank argues that this means even a continuation of the current situation carries upside risk, with a higher chance of a sharp price spike than before.

Two other indicators support that view. Demand from the most price-sensitive buyers is recovering, with combined China and India seaborne imports climbing back toward year-earlier levels after a deep slump. And speculative positioning in Brent and WTI remains light, which leaves room for buyers to return.

Barclays also addressed the recent widening in the price gap between WTI and Canadian heavy crude. It said the gap reflects shipping costs, refinery and upgrader outages and strategic reserve releases, not a surge in supply. The bank kept its price forecasts unchanged and repeated its recommendation for long calendar spreads in Brent, a bet that near-dated contracts will gain against later ones as supplies stay tight. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6756 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed’s Williams says inflation stubbornly high and Fed still has work to do on policy
item.description:
Williams’ remarks support pricing for a December hike and the dollar’s rate advantage, keeping front-end Treasury yields firm. His emphasis on acting “over time” and on a steady, data-led approach suggests no urgency for a half-point move, which may limit how far bets on a larger hike can build. The comments add to pressure on gold, which has been falling as hike expectations push up real yields. Higher-for-longer messaging also keeps oil-driven inflation risk at the centre of the policy outlook.

---

Williams says the Fed has more tightening to do but suggests a steady pace, which supports a December hike without adding much to bets on a bigger move.

Summary:

  • New York Fed President Williams says inflation is too high and stubbornly persistent
  • He says the Fed will need to act over time to bring inflation back to its 2% target
  • In his view, the Fed still has work to do to get monetary policy to the right place
  • He describes the US economy as resilient, with strong growth, getting stronger but not overheating
  • He says the Fed has been collecting data at a steady cadence
  • The remarks follow this week’s hotter-than-expected October CPI and come ahead of the 9 December Fed decision

New York Fed President John Williams said inflation remains too high and the Federal Reserve still has work to do to get monetary policy to the right place, reinforcing expectations that the central bank will keep raising interest rates. Speaking on a panel at a UC Berkeley alumni event in New York on Thursday evening (2330 GMT), Williams described inflation as stubbornly persistent. He said the Fed will need to take action over time to bring it back to its 2% target.

Williams was confident about the economy. He said it has been resilient and growth has been strong, and that the US economy is getting stronger but is not overheating. That combination matters for the policy debate. A solid economy gives the Fed room to tighten further without tipping growth into reverse, while the absence of overheating suggests he does not see a need to rush.

He also said the Fed has been collecting data at a steady cadence, language that points to a methodical, meeting-by-meeting approach rather than a sudden change of pace. His comment that action will be needed “over time” suggests he supports continued, gradual tightening.

The remarks come two days after a hotter-than-expected October consumer price report. Headline prices rose 0.4% on the month and core prices 0.3%, both above forecasts. Since then, markets have priced a high probability of a quarter-point hike at the Fed’s 9 December decision, along with an outside chance of a half-point move. Fed Governor Christopher Waller has said he would favour a quarter-point hike in December and could prefer a larger step if inflation runs hotter than expected.

In the comments reported, Williams did not commit to a specific move in December. But he is a permanent voter and vice chair of the Federal Open Market Committee, so his views carry significant weight. His message is also in line with his remarks in Frankfurt a week earlier, when he called inflation far too high.

For markets, the comments support the case for a December hike without encouraging bets on a larger move. The next test is the data due before the meeting, especially further inflation readings, which will decide whether “over time” means one hike or several. 

December pre-Christmas rate hike coming up!

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US Treasury bought yen in July, its first intervention since 1998, as yen nears 160 again
item.description:
The report confirms that the US is a willing partner in yen support, not just a bystander. That raises the risk for anyone betting heavily on dollar-yen above 160, a level that now looks well defended. Positioning is likely to turn more cautious as the pair approaches the summer’s intervention zone, and volatility could spike on any further rate checks. Rate expectations still favour the dollar, though, because the US economy is resilient and inflation is high. That means intervention may only slow the yen’s slide unless the BOJ follows through with a December hike to 1.5%.

---

Yesterday:

  • Japan’s Mimura warns yen moves are too rapid as USD/JPY pushes back toward 160

---

Washington has now confirmed that it put its own money behind the yen this summer. With the currency back near 160, the main question is whether Tokyo and Washington can hold that line again.

Summary:

  • The New York Fed bought about 79bn yen (roughly $500m) on 31 July for the US Treasury, the first US yen-buying intervention since 1998
  • The Fed made no foreign exchange interventions on its own account in the July to September quarter
  • Japan’s Ministry of Finance intervened with about 15trn yen in coordination, and dollar-yen fell from around 164 to around 155 in a few days
  • Rate checks on 30 July were carried out solely for the Treasury, and the yen rose more than 2% that day
  • The yen has since weakened back toward 160, and Japanese officials warn that the intervention should not be forgotten
  • Most economists expect the BOJ to raise rates to 1.5% in December

The US Treasury bought Japanese yen in the third quarter, its first yen-buying intervention since 1998, while the Federal Reserve did not intervene in currency markets on its own account, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York said on Thursday. The New York Fed’s quarterly report on foreign exchange operations confirms that Washington acted alongside Tokyo this summer to stop a sharp slide in the Japanese currency, Reuters reported.

According to the report, the New York Fed bought about 79 billion yen, worth roughly $500 million, in the spot market on 31 July. It paid with euros from the Treasury’s Exchange Stabilization Fund, and said the purchase was made to counter what the Treasury saw as disorderly moves in the yen. Rate checks on dollar-yen had been reported on 30 July. These are calls to dealers asking for prices, and markets often read them as a sign that intervention is coming. The report said the New York Fed made those checks solely on the Treasury’s behalf, acting as its fiscal agent. The yen rose more than 2% that day.

Japan’s Ministry of Finance intervened at the same time, spending about 15 trillion yen during the quarter. The combined action worked quickly: between 30 July and 3 August, dollar-yen fell from around 164 to around 155. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in early August that the US would not hesitate to join further intervention, and repeated his call for the Bank of Japan to keep raising interest rates.

The yen’s recovery has not lasted. It has drifted back toward 160 per dollar, its weakest level since September. On Thursday, Atsushi Mimura, Japan’s vice finance minister for international affairs and its top currency diplomat, warned that it was too early to forget the summer’s intervention. Analysts at Mizuho Securities expect the dollar to keep rising against the yen, supported by a resilient US economy and inflation kept high by strong AI investment, and flagged the risk of fresh action by Japan.

The Bank of Japan is the other tool available. Some BOJ policymakers called in October for faster rate rises, arguing that underlying inflation has reached the 2% target. Most economists in a Reuters poll expect the bank to raise its policy rate to 1.5% in December, after hikes in June and September. Now that the US is on record as a willing partner, any renewed push toward 160 and beyond is likely to meet stronger resistance from both governments.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BlackRock sees gold support intact despite near 30% drop from record, expects milder gains
item.description:
BlackRock’s view backs the idea that gold’s correction has been driven by rates, not by fading long-term demand. Near-term direction depends mainly on real yields and the dollar. With markets pricing further Fed tightening, rallies are likely to be hard to sustain, and gold has tended to fall rather than rise as geopolitical risk lifts oil, inflation and hike expectations. Central bank buying offers some support on dips, but BlackRock expects that buying to slow from its recent pace. Silver remains the more cyclical and riskier of the two, more exposed to swings in industrial demand and growth expectations.

---

Earlier

  • Three drivers setting gold’s tone as December Fed hike bets build, according to Standard Chartered

---

BlackRock says gold’s structural support from central banks is intact, but with real yields and the dollar working against it, investors should expect it to stabilise portfolios rather than repeat last year’s surge.

Summary:

  • Gold is around $3,870/oz, about 28% below its record near $5,400 on 29 January
  • The pullback reflects the unwinding of debasement trades as US growth rebounded, real yields rose and the dollar strengthened
  • Central banks bought more than 3,900 tonnes between 2022 and the first half of 2026, and a record 45% plan to add more
  • Gold has overtaken US Treasuries as the largest share of global reserves for the first time in about 30 years
  • Since 2020, gold has returned about 2% on average in months when the S&P 500 fell more than 5%
  • Silver is around $52, more than 55% below its January record near $118, and around 60% of its demand is industrial

Gold’s long-term case is still intact after a sharp pullback from its January record, but investors should expect steadier, more moderate returns rather than a repeat of the past year’s surge, according to BlackRock. In a note published on 10 November, Kristy Akullian, head of iShares investment strategy for the Americas, described the outlook for precious metals as more balanced, with near-term headwinds now offsetting longer-term support.

Gold hit a record of around $5,400 an ounce on 29 January. Based on BlackRock’s data, it had fallen about 23% from that peak by mid-October. The decline has continued since, and gold now trades around $3,870, roughly 28% below the high. The firm puts much of the fall down to the unwinding of so-called debasement trades. Worries about rising government debt had pushed investors into hard assets. As US growth rebounded, real yields rose and the dollar strengthened, the focus shifted, and gold lost ground along with digital assets.

Those same forces remain the main near-term obstacle. Gold pays no income, so higher real yields and a firmer dollar raise the cost of holding it. That backdrop is unlikely to ease quickly while markets are pricing further Fed tightening.

BlackRock argues that the longer-term support comes mainly from central banks. They hold about a fifth of all gold ever mined and bought more than 3,900 tonnes between 2022 and the first half of 2026. Gold has also overtaken US Treasuries as the largest share of global reserves for the first time in three decades. In a 2026 survey, a record 45% of central banks said they plan to add to their own holdings. BlackRock expects that buying to slow from its recent pace but to remain an important support. A newer source of demand is stablecoin issuers, some of which now hold gold as reserves.

BlackRock presents gold as a portfolio stabiliser rather than a trade. Since 2020, gold has returned about 2% on average in months when the S&P 500 fell more than 5%, while bonds were broadly flat.

Silver has been far more volatile. It hit a record near $118 in January and now trades around $52, more than 55% below that peak, a reminder that its swings have historically been up to twice the size of gold’s. Around 60% of silver demand comes from electronics, solar and semiconductors. That gives it more upside in a strong economy, but more downside when growth weakens.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: UBS sees no RBA cuts until late 2027 as AI boom fuels inflation, growth slowing to 1.4%
item.description:
UBS’s view is more hawkish than current market pricing, which has moved towards RBA cuts within months. That leaves front-end Australian bond yields exposed if upcoming inflation data run hot. For the Australian dollar, a longer restrictive period would support rate differentials, but the weak domestic growth outlook limits how much it can benefit. The February RBA meeting is now a live risk if quarterly core inflation stays near a 1% pace. UBS’s upbeat global outlook depends partly on a Middle East resolution bringing oil prices down, so a lasting oil shock would hurt both growth and the inflation outlook.

--- UBS says the AI boom is giving Australia the inflation now and the productivity later, which means no RBA cuts until late 2027 and a private sector that will feel like it’s in recession.

Summary:

  • UBS expects the RBA to stay restrictive through much of 2027, with cuts unlikely before late 2027 or 2028
  • In the near term, another hike is more likely than a cut, with February in play if inflation surprises to the upside
  • Data centre investment has risen about tenfold in three years, but there is little evidence yet of productivity gains
  • Australian growth is forecast to slow to about 1.4% in 2027, below most forecasts and slightly under the RBA’s
  • Official household spending growth of 6% to 7% looks at odds with listed retailers’ near-flat trading updates
  • UBS forecasts global growth of about 3.5% in 2027, above consensus, if the AI boom holds and the Middle East conflict is resolved

The AI investment boom is adding to Australia’s inflation problem before it delivers any productivity gains, and that is likely to keep the Reserve Bank of Australia’s policy restrictive well into 2027, according to UBS. The bank’s chief economist for Australasia, George Tharenou, told ausbiz he does not expect rate cuts until late 2027 or 2028. He said that if the RBA does move in the near term, another hike is more likely than a cut.

Tharenou said a recent speech by RBA Assistant Governor Sarah Hunter (RBA’s Hunter warns AI could trigger sharp asset repricing as boom adds to inflation ) showed how seriously the central bank is taking the AI shock. The RBA estimates data centre investment has risen about tenfold in three years, and the pipeline of approved projects could see it double again. The eventual productivity gain could be anywhere from 0.1% to 2% a year, but so far there is little evidence of it. For now, Tharenou argued, AI is acting as a demand shock in an economy where capacity is already tight and inflation is too high. That raises the neutral interest rate and argues for tighter policy for longer.

That puts UBS at odds with markets, which turned dovish after the RBA’s last meeting and started pricing cuts within months. UBS’s central case is an extended hold. But Tharenou flagged the February meeting as a possible hike if inflation surprises to the upside, particularly if quarterly core inflation runs near a 1% pace. He noted that several board members voted against hiking last time, so it would probably take a clear inflation surprise to change their minds.

On growth, UBS expects Australia’s economy to slow to about 1.4% in 2027, below most forecasts and slightly under the RBA’s. AI investment could add up to half a percentage point and government spending remains strong, which makes a technical recession hard to bring about. But outside the AI boom, Tharenou expects the private sector to be close to flat, with falling house prices weighing on consumers and unemployment rising above 5%. In his view, it will feel like a recession even if the data don’t show one.

He also questioned the strength of official household spending figures, which have been growing at around 6% to 7% a year, while listed retailers’ trading updates point to growth close to flat. He expects the official numbers to slow sharply over the coming year.

UBS is more upbeat about the world economy, forecasting global growth of about 3.5% in 2027, above consensus. That depends on the AI boom continuing and a resolution in the Middle East bringing oil prices down.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Anthropic IPO targets around $1 trillion valuation, half the $2 trillion once whispered
item.description:
A listing of this size will test how much appetite there is for AI risk after the recent tech selloff. Strong demand would suggest investors still see value in leading AI names at lower valuations. The roughly $87bn raised between the public offering and the strategic placement could pull money away from other tech holdings in the run-up to pricing. Strategic investors Nvidia, Micron, Alphabet and Microsoft are also tied to the deal, so a strong debut could support the wider AI infrastructure trade. A weak one would likely weigh on it.

-

Earlier:

  • Anthropic reserves up to 20% of its $64 billion IPO for retail investors
  • Anthropic IPO oversubscribed several times ahead of record $90 billion listing

- Anthropic is coming to market at about half the valuation once talked about, with very fast growth and a large cash pile, but also with compute commitments that will test whether that growth can last.

Summary:

  • 825 million shares are to be priced at $70 to $78 on 18 November, with Nasdaq trading as ANT from 19 November
  • The midpoint raises about $61bn and values the company at around $1trn, or about $1.2trn fully diluted
  • About $26bn of extra stock goes to strategic investors including Microsoft, Nvidia, Alphabet and Micron
  • Q3 revenue rose more than 12-fold to about $17bn, with an adjusted operating margin of 15% and a long-term target of 35%
  • Up to 20% of the deal is reserved for retail investors, with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley leading the underwriting
  • Cash of about $132bn is expected to rise to around $210bn after the IPO, against about $900bn of compute commitments through 2045

Anthropic is set to list on Nasdaq next week at a valuation of around $1 trillion. That is well below the $2 trillion figure some on Wall Street had talked about before a run of AI-led selloffs hit technology stocks. The maker of the Claude AI assistant plans to sell 825 million shares at $70 to $78 each. Pricing is expected on 18 November, with trading under the ticker ANT due to start the following day.

At the midpoint of the range, the offering would raise about $61 billion, Barron’s reported, citing the company’s filing and an investor presentation. Anthropic will also sell around $26 billion of stock at the IPO price to a group of strategic investors that includes Microsoft, Nvidia, Alphabet and Micron Technology. With about 13.1 billion shares outstanding, the midpoint implies a value of roughly $1 trillion, or about $1.2 trillion on a fully diluted basis.

The growth numbers behind that price are steep. Third-quarter revenue rose more than 12-fold from a year earlier to about $17 billion, and October sales reached an annualised run rate of around $80 billion. The company reported an adjusted operating margin of 15% in the quarter, against an operating loss a year earlier, and is targeting 35% over the long term. That values the company at roughly 12 to 13 times October’s annualised sales, a multiple that would shrink quickly if growth holds.

Investors will need to look past the headline GAAP figures. As Anthropic’s private valuation rose, so did the value of convertible securities issued to early investors, and accounting rules treat that increase as a loss. That noncash charge came to about $94 billion over the first nine months of 2026, and the company strips it out of its adjusted results. The convertibles will be swapped for common stock at the IPO.

The deal also stands out for how much goes to retail investors. Up to 20% of the shares are set aside for individuals. They will be sold through the main underwriting group, led by Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, and through retail brokers such as Robinhood, Charles Schwab and Fidelity. Reports say the deal is heavily oversubscribed, so many retail buyers may get small allocations or none at all.

Anthropic goes into the listing with about $132 billion of cash and no conventional debt, a figure expected to rise to around $210 billion after the offering. The bigger risks are competition and the scale of its spending commitments. Rivals include OpenAI, Alphabet, Meta and, in particular, lower-cost open-weight models from China. The company has signed up to about $900 billion of computing commitments through 2045, including $29 billion due in 2027. Whether it can keep growing fast enough to cover those costs and reach its margin target is the question the market will start pricing next week.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman sees AI spending hitting $1.4 trillion by end-2027, nearly 4% of the US economy
item.description:
Goldman’s forecast supports the AI infrastructure trade, especially chipmakers, chip equipment makers and networking suppliers, which get the most from a spending path well above consensus. Its point that most AI hardware is imported matters for macro traders. Strong capex does not mean equally strong US GDP growth, and the gap shows up instead in a wider trade deficit and in demand for Asian supply chains. Downplaying the regulatory risk from the midterms may ease one worry that has weighed on data centre-linked stocks. Funding costs remain the main pressure point, as Fed hike expectations push borrowing costs higher.

---

Earlier:

  • Cerebras raises 2026 outlook, sees revenue tripling in 2027 as $26bn backlog builds
  • Applied Materials beats on Q4 and guides above forecasts as chip equipment demand holds
  • Cisco beats and lifts FY27 view as AI revenue from hyperscalers set to more than double

---

Goldman expects AI spending to reach a $1.4 trillion annual pace by the end of 2027 and keep driving US capex, but because much of the hardware is imported, the direct boost to US GDP is far smaller than the spending total.

Summary:

  • Annualised AI-related hardware and IP spending is seen at $1.4trn by the end of 2027, nearly 4% of the US economy
  • Spending is expected to pass $900bn by the end of 2026
  • US business investment is forecast to grow about 8% in 2027, nearly double the consensus of around 4%
  • AI is expected to add more than 5 percentage points to 2027 capex growth, but only 0.6 point to GDP including semiconductors and 0.2 point without them
  • Most information processing equipment is imported and so netted out of GDP
  • Democrats’ midterm wins are seen posing only limited risks to AI investment; rising borrowing costs are the bigger risk

Artificial intelligence will remain the main driver of US business investment growth in 2027, according to Goldman Sachs. The bank expects annualised spending on AI-related hardware and intellectual property to reach $1.4 trillion by the end of next year, equivalent to nearly 4% of the US economy. That compares with its forecast of more than $900 billion by the end of 2026, Reuters reported on Wednesday.

The outlook is well above the market consensus. Goldman expects US business investment to grow about 8% in 2027, close to double the consensus forecast of around 4%. It estimates that AI-related investment alone will add more than 5 percentage points to capex growth next year once semiconductors are included.

The more striking detail is how little of that spending shows up in US output. Goldman estimates AI investment will add 0.6 percentage point to US GDP growth in 2027 including semiconductors, and only 0.2 point without them. The reason is trade: most information processing equipment is imported, so it is netted out of GDP. The bank also argued that official business investment data undercount semiconductor investment. In other words, the AI boom is huge for capex and for the companies supplying it, but its direct boost to the US economy is much smaller than the spending total suggests.

On politics, Goldman played down the risk from Democrats’ victories in this month’s midterm elections, which had raised concerns about tighter regulation of data centre development. The bank said the outcome poses only limited risks to AI investment.

The forecast comes in a week when corporate results have backed the spending story. Cisco raised its full-year outlook on strong AI networking demand from hyperscalers, Applied Materials guided above forecasts on chip equipment orders, and Cerebras reported a backlog of around $26 billion.

The main risk is funding. Rising borrowing costs and tighter investor scrutiny could slow AI capital spending, particularly as companies rely more on debt to pay for the build-out. With markets pricing a strong chance of another Fed hike in December, the cost of that debt is worth watching.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
